title: What Americans Need to Know About Traveling to Canada Amid the Escalating Trade War
excerpt: Despite doubling auto tariffs and collapsed trade talks, US-Canada borders remain open for tourists — but the broader chill in cross-border travel is reshaping North American tourism.
body:
• US-Canada borders remain fully open for tourists, and US citizens can enter Canada with a passport or NEXUS card without a visa for stays under 180 days.
  • Tariffs primarily affect manufactured and agricultural goods — travel industry experts say they will not directly increase the cost of trips for American tourists visiting Canada.
  • Canadian tourist arrivals to the US dropped 20.9% in 2025, while American departures to Canada fell 4.7% — the first decline since the pandemic began in 2020.
  • President Trump announced he would double tariffs on Canadian automobiles to 50% starting January 1, after trade talks between the two countries collapsed last week.

Borders Open, Trade Talks Collapsed

The US-Canada trade war escalated sharply this week after negotiations between the two countries broke down. President Donald Trump announced on August 24 that he would double tariffs on automobiles and car parts imported from Canada to 50%, effective January 1. The announcement came days after 50% tariffs on a separate category of Canadian goods — including dairy, wine, and hockey sticks — took effect on August 22.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney responded by saying Canada would implement retaliatory tariffs in September.

For the millions of Americans who cross into Canada each year — for vacation, family visits, or business — the question on many minds is straightforward: will my trip cost more?

Tariffs Target Goods, Not Services

The short answer, according to trade and tourism experts, is probably not.

"There's no direct causation I can see caused by this trade negotiation between the US and Canada, because it's mainly about the manufacturing goods and the agricultural goods," Jungho Suh, Assistant Professor of Management at George Washington University's School of Business, told USA TODAY.

Suh said he did not expect the latest escalation to directly impact the cost of trips for American travelers. The tariffs target imported physical goods — car parts, dairy products, lumber — not the service sector that drives tourism, including hotels, restaurants, and local transportation.

"The current negotiations between the US and Canada, and the tariff issue, all these things are not new factors from the companies' perspective."

— Jungho Suh, George Washington University

The Real Impact: Sentiment, Not Prices

While trip costs may not change much, the political climate is already reshaping cross-border travel patterns. Canadian visitors have been staying home in large numbers. The US had just over 6.5 million visitor arrivals from Canada through May 2026, down 9.3% year over year, according to the Department of Commerce's National Travel and Tourism Office.

The broader trend is even starker. There were roughly 4.2 million fewer Canadian visitor arrivals to the US in all of 2025 compared with the previous year — a 20.9% drop. A Joint Economic Committee report found that passenger vehicles crossing the US-Canada border declined by nearly 20% from January to October 2025, with some border states seeing declines as large as 27%.

Some Canadians are avoiding the US altogether, citing reasons including Trump expressing interest in making Canada "the 51st state" and recent detainments of Canadian tourists at US border crossings. An Angus Reid poll found 70% of Canadians were uneasy about visiting the US.

Americans Are Also Traveling Less to Canada

The chill cuts both ways. US outbound departures to Canada fell 4.7% in 2025 to 13.4 million — the first decline since 2020, when the COVID-19 pandemic shut down international travel, according to data the International Trade Administration shared with USA TODAY.

Tourism industry groups estimate that even a 10% reduction in Canadian tourism to the US would mean a $2.1 billion drop in spending and the loss of 14,000 American jobs. An expanded trade war could result in a $22 billion loss in tourism revenue from international visitors, according to the research firm Tourism Economics.

What Travelers Should Know

For Americans planning trips to Canada, the practical guidance is reassuring. Borders remain open. No visa is required for stays under 180 days. A valid US passport book, passport card, or NEXUS card is sufficient for entry.

For Indian-Americans who frequently travel between the US and Canada for family, business, or leisure, the primary concern is not cost but the broader geopolitical uncertainty. Indian nationals traveling on US green cards or visas should ensure their travel documents are current and carry proof of US residency status when crossing the border.
